name: House piano loop
notes: Sevenths on every chord and no dominant, which keeps a four-bar loop from wearing out over eight minutes. Stab the chords on the offbeats and leave the downbeats to the kick.

name: Trance lift
notes: Two bars a chord climbing into the tonic halfway through, then on to the relative major. Eight bars is long enough that the arrival in bar five reads as an event rather than a repeat.

name: Arpeggiator minor
notes: Descending by step then jumping up a fifth to the relative major, so the last chord resets the line. Written for a sixteenth-note arpeggio, where the chord shape matters more than the voicing.

name: Synthwave drive
notes: Two bars a chord, climbing from bVI through bVII and landing on the relative major rather than coming home. The slow harmonic rhythm is what makes it feel like cruising rather than running.

name: Four to the floor
notes: The descending minor line with a dominant seventh at the bottom instead of a plain triad, so it slams back to the tonic every four bars. The raised seventh in V7 is the only chromatic note.

name: Ambient drift
notes: Four bars of tonic before anything moves, then II7 supplies the raised fourth and vi7 takes it away again. The change is a shift of colour rather than a move anywhere.

name: Minimal techno
notes: One chord for eight bars. Everything that happens has to happen in the rhythm, the filter and the arrangement, which is the discipline the style is built on.

name: Garage two-step
notes: Two bars on the tonic then two chords in the last two bars, so the loop is weighted at the front. The maj7 at the end is the brightest thing in it and sets up the return.

name: Indie jangle
notes: Ending on ii rather than V leaves the loop unresolved without needing a dominant anywhere. Play it with a capo and open shapes so the top strings ring through the changes.

name: Shoegaze wash
notes: A borrowed bVII against a sus2 tonic, so neither end of the loop has a clear third. Two bars a chord under enough reverb that the changes overlap on purpose.

name: Post-punk drive
notes: Two bars of tonic, then the Neapolitan a semitone above and bVII a tone below, so the last bar pulls in the opposite direction to the one before it. Keep the bass running eighths and do not resolve it.

name: Dream pop lift
notes: The tonic never appears, so the loop hovers around it without ever landing. IV at both ends makes the phrase circular rather than directional.

name: Math rock in seven
notes: Seven quavers a bar over four otherwise ordinary chords, so the metre carries all the difficulty. Group it three-two-two and let the tapped figure repeat across the bar line.

name: Bedroom pop
notes: Sevenths on all four chords with the bass rising in thirds, which blurs the boundaries between them. Nothing here has any urgency, which is the register the style works in.

name: Lo-fi loop
notes: A two-five that resolves deceptively to iii7 and then vi7 rather than to the tonic. The tonic never arrives, which is why it loops indefinitely without feeling like a repeat.

name: Chillwave
notes: Mixolydian with a maj7 tonic, so the chord has both a major seventh and a scale with a flat one around it. That contradiction is most of the haze.

name: Drum and bass minor
notes: Four bars of tonic before anything moves, which leaves room for the break to be the event. The last four bars climb back up so the loop restarts under its own momentum.

name: Electro swing
notes: Two chords a bar cadencing twice, which gives a sampled loop somewhere obvious to cut. The diminished ii and the dominant do the same job from slightly different angles.

name: Indie folk capo shapes
notes: The axis with a major seventh on IV, which on guitar means lifting one finger rather than learning a chord. Capo up and use G-shape fingerings so the open strings do the ringing.

name: Slacker rock
notes: Two borrowed chords from the parallel minor alternating with two from the key, so it flickers between bright and flat. No dominant, and no interest in resolving.

name: Motorik
notes: Four bars each on two chords a whole tone apart, at a steady eighth-note pulse that never varies. The point is repetition long enough that the listener stops tracking the change.

name: Glitch in five
notes: Five beats a bar with a chord change on each downbeat, so the harmony is regular and the pulse is not. Count two plus three to make it lope rather than stumble.

name: Future garage
notes: Starting on iv7 puts the tonic in bar five rather than bar one, so the loop feels like it is always halfway through. Major sevenths on the two borrowed chords keep the edges soft.

name: Indie anthem in six
notes: Six bars of 6/8 that run partway through the canon sequence and stop on V. The odd phrase length means it never sits square against a four-bar drum pattern.

name: Vaporwave slow
notes: The doo-wop changes with sevenths, in 12/8, at a tempo slow enough to feel wrong. Slowing an ordinary progression down until it drags is most of what the genre does.
